preview_text: ตกขาวไม่ใช่เงื่อนไขเดียว แต่เป็นแผนผังภูมิทัศน์ภายในของคุณ สี เนื้อสัมผัส และจังหวะเวลาเผยให้เห็นว่ารากเป็นเลือดนิ่ง ความร้อนชื้น หรือความเย็นลึก...
conventional_description: In Western medicine, brown vaginal discharge is often considered old blood mixed with normal vaginal secretions. It can occur at the beginning or end of a period, during ovulation, or as a side effect of hormonal contraceptives. While occasional brown spotting is usually harmless, persistent or foul-smelling discharge may indicate an infection (such as bacterial vaginosis or pelvic inflammatory disease), endometrial polyps, or other gynecological conditions. Diagnosis typically involves a pelvic exam, swabs, and sometimes ultrasound.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment depends on the underlying cause. For infections, antibiotics or antifungals are prescribed. Hormonal imbalances may be managed with oral contraceptives or other hormone therapies. If structural issues like polyps are present, minor surgery may be recommended. For many women with unexplained brown discharge, no specific treatment is offered beyond watchful waiting.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, vaginal discharge is governed by the Ren (Conception) and Dai (Girdle) channels. These energetic pathways are responsible for holding the uterus and its secretions in place. When they are weakened or disturbed, abnormal discharge appears. Brown discharge specifically points to old blood - blood that has lingered and oxidized - rather than fresh bleeding. This old blood is a clue that something is obstructing its normal flow or that heat is 'cooking' it inside the body.
One common cause is Blood Stagnation with Heat. Emotional stress, surgery, or chronic inflammation can cause blood to congeal in the pelvic vessels. Over time, this stagnant blood breaks down and is expelled as dark, sometimes clotted discharge. The heat that accompanies the stagnation makes the blood darker and the pain sharper, often felt as a fixed stabbing sensation.
Another major cause is Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner. When the Spleen is weak - often from a diet heavy in greasy, sweet, or spicy foods - it fails to transform fluids. Dampness accumulates, combines with heat, and sinks downward. This produces a sticky, brownish-yellow discharge with a foul odor and a heavy, dragging feeling in the lower abdomen.
Emotional factors play a role too. Long-standing frustration or anger can cause Liver Qi to stagnate and generate heat, which then disturbs the Ren and Dai channels. And when Kidney Yin - the body's deep cooling reserve - is depleted by overwork or aging, empty heat rises and scorches the channels, leading to a scant, brownish-red discharge with night sweats and dry mouth. Each of these patterns requires a different treatment strategy, which is why TCM doesn't offer a one-size-fits-all remedy.
classical_quote: 「夫赤带亦湿病，湿是土之气，宜见黄白之色，今不见黄白而见赤者，火热故也。火色赤，故带下亦赤耳。」
classical_translation: "Red leukorrhea is also a dampness disease. Dampness corresponds to the Earth phase and should manifest as yellow or white discharge. When it appears red instead, it is due to fire-heat. Fire is red, hence the discharge is red. This passage explains that red or brownish discharge arises when dampness combines with heat, and the treatment must clear heat and dry dampness simultaneously."
classical_source:
Fu Qing Zhu Nu Ke (Fu Qingzhu's Obstetrics and Gynecology)  ,  Section on Leukorrhea (带下), Chapter: Red Leukorrhea (赤带) 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking about the color, consistency, and timing of the discharge, as well as any other symptoms that appear alongside it. Brownish discharge often signals old blood stasis or a combination of dampness and heat, rather than fresh heat alone. The source of the stagnation or dampness - whether from emotional stress, a weak Spleen, Yin deficiency, or congealed Blood - determines which pattern is active.
If the discharge is dark brown, possibly clotted, and accompanied by fixed, stabbing lower abdominal pain, Blood Stagnation with Heat is the key consideration. The tongue often looks purplish or has dark spots, and the pulse may feel choppy. Questions about the regularity of periods and the presence of clots help confirm that Heat has congealed the Blood.
When the discharge is sticky, brownish-yellow, and has a foul odor, Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner is the likely culprit. The practitioner will ask about a sensation of heaviness in the lower abdomen, urinary discomfort, or a greasy taste in the mouth. The tongue usually has a thick, yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse feels slippery and rapid, signaling the combined presence of Dampness and Heat.
If the discharge is brownish-red and appears or worsens during periods of high stress, irritability, or frustration, the practitioner suspects Liver Qi Stagnation transforming into Heat. The tongue may show red sides, and the pulse often feels wiry and rapid. Questions about mood and menstrual regularity help confirm that emotional tension is the trigger.
For a scanty, bright-red or brown discharge that appears alongside night sweats, a dry mouth, or hot flashes, Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat Blazing is the focus. The tongue is typically red with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. The practitioner will ask about sleep quality and any sensation of heat in the palms or soles to distinguish this from other patterns.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed stabbing lower abdominal pain", "Dark-brown or clotted discharge", "Pain worse at night and with pressure", "Sensation of internal heat, especially at night", "Irritability and restlessness"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Stress and anger, Hot weather, Prolonged sitting
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement, Cooling foods and drinks, Rest and lying down, Emotional stability
patterns.why_this_happens: When Heat enters the Blood, it thickens and congeals the blood, leading to stagnation in the uterine vessels. This stagnant blood breaks down and is discharged as dark-brown, sometimes clotted, discharge. The stasis itself creates a fixed, stabbing pain in the lower abdomen, while the lingering Heat causes restlessness and a sensation of internal warmth, especially at night.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin dry yellow coating. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) and rapid (数 shuò), often wiry (弦 xián) at the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol generate internal heat and dampness, which thicken the blood and worsen stasis. Emotional stress constrains Liver Qi, generating heat and further congealing blood. Prolonged sitting blocks the flow of Qi and blood in the lower burner, while gentle movement helps circulate blood and relieve stasis. Cooling foods and rest reduce internal heat, easing the dark discharge and pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, fried, and greasy foods that generate heat. Include cooling, blood-nourishing foods like cucumber, celery, and mung beans. Gentle movement such as walking or yoga helps circulate Qi and blood. Manage stress and anger to prevent Qi stagnation.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it fails to transform fluids, and dampness builds up. Over time, this dampness combines with heat - often from a diet rich in greasy or spicy foods, or from external damp-heat - and sinks downward to the lower burner. The heat damages the Ren and Dai channels, causing the discharge to take on a brownish-yellow color and a foul smell, while the dampness makes it sticky and heavy.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow greasy coating, thickest at the root. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), more pronounced at the rear position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat thrives on moisture and heat. Greasy, spicy foods and alcohol directly add dampness and heat to the body, making the discharge heavier and more odorous. A humid environment mirrors the pattern's internal climate, worsening symptoms. On the other hand, cooling, bland foods help the body drain excess dampness and cool the heat, while light movement keeps Qi and fluids moving so they don't stagnate in the lower burner.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, cooling foods that drain dampness - barley, mung beans, cucumber, and celery are excellent. Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, or sugary foods, and cut out alcohol, as they generate more dampness and heat. Wear breathable cotton underwear and avoid sitting for long periods in damp or hot environments.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney Yin Deficiency With Empty-Heat Blazing
patterns.symptoms: ["Scant, brownish-red discharge, no foul odor", "Night sweats", "Five-palm heat (heat in palms, soles, and chest)", "Dry mouth and throat, especially at night", "Lower back soreness and weakness", "Tinnitus or diminished hearing"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and lack of sleep, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Emotional stress and frustration, Excessive sexual activity
patterns.better_with: Adequate sleep, Cooling foods and drinks, Gentle movement
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yin is the body's cooling reserve. When it runs low over time, empty heat rises because there is not enough Yin to anchor the Yang. This empty heat travels upward and disturbs the Ren and Dai channels, the vessels that govern the uterus and vaginal discharge. The heat scorches the fluids and tints the discharge a brownish or bright-red color, but the amount is typically scant because the Yin fluids are depleted.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry with little or no coating; cracks may appear. Pulse: fine (Xi) and rapid (Shu), weak especially at the rear (Chi) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is depleted by anything that overheats or overuses the body's reserves. Late nights, overwork, and excessive sexual activity directly consume Yin, while spicy and fried foods generate internal heat that further dries up fluids. Rest, cooling foods, and gentle movement allow the body to rebuild Yin and calm the empty heat, so the Dai channel can regain its normal function and the discharge stops.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid late nights, which consume Yin. Eat moistening, cooling foods like pear, black sesame, goji berries, and millet. Avoid spicy, fried, or overly heating foods and alcohol. Gentle exercise like tai chi or walking supports Yin without overheating the body.

faqs.question: Is brown discharge always a sign of a serious problem?
faqs.answer: Not always. In TCM, brown discharge is seen as a sign of an internal imbalance, but it doesn't necessarily mean you have a dangerous disease. It often reflects old blood being expelled, which can be due to stagnation or heat. However, if the discharge is accompanied by severe pain, fever, heavy bleeding, or occurs during pregnancy, you should seek urgent medical care. For persistent but mild discharge, a TCM evaluation can help identify the underlying pattern and address it before it worsens.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my doctor says everything is normal?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is a common scenario. Many women are told their discharge is 'normal' after standard tests come back negative, yet the symptom persists. TCM excels at treating these functional imbalances that don't show up on lab tests. By looking at your overall pattern - your tongue, pulse, emotions, and accompanying symptoms - a practitioner can identify whether damp-heat, blood stasis, or a deficiency is at play and create a personalized treatment plan to restore balance.

faqs.question: How long does it take for herbs to stop the discharge?
faqs.answer: Most women notice a reduction in discharge within the first 2-4 weeks of herbal treatment. The color often lightens first, then the volume decreases. For patterns rooted in deficiency (like Kidney Yin Deficiency), it may take 2-3 months to fully resolve because the body needs time to rebuild its reserves. Consistency is key - take your herbs as prescribed and attend weekly acupuncture sessions for the best results.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside antibiotics or hormonal contraceptives?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. TCM herbal formulas can complement antibiotic treatment for infections by helping clear damp-heat and supporting your body's recovery. If you're on hormonal contraceptives, there are no known direct interactions, though your practitioner may note any influence on your pattern. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking. If you are on blood thinners, discuss with both, as some blood-moving herbs may interact.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role in TCM treatment for vaginal discharge. You'll likely be advised to avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and overly sweet foods, as well as alcohol and excessive dairy, because these create dampness and heat. Instead, favor light, cooked meals with plenty of vegetables and whole grains. Specific recommendations will depend on your pattern - for example, someone with damp-heat might focus on cooling foods like mung beans, while someone with deficiency might add nourishing foods like black sesame.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture hurt for pelvic issues?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture needles are extremely thin, and most people feel only a mild sensation - often described as a dull ache or tingling - rather than pain. Points on the lower abdomen and legs are commonly used for pelvic conditions, and the treatment is generally very relaxing. Many patients even fall asleep during their session. The goal is to move stagnant energy and blood gently, not to cause discomfort.

faqs.question: What's the difference between brown discharge and spotting?
faqs.answer: Spotting usually refers to small amounts of fresh red or pink blood between periods, while brown discharge is older blood that has oxidized and turned brown. In TCM, spotting often indicates a failure of the Spleen to hold blood or heat in the blood, whereas brown discharge more specifically points to blood stasis or damp-heat. Both can be addressed with Chinese medicine, but the herbal formulas and acupuncture points used may differ based on the color and accompanying symptoms.

research.title: Clinical observation on modified Longdan Xiegan Decoction in treating chronic cervicitis with damp-heat syndrome
research.description: A randomized controlled trial of 120 patients with chronic cervicitis and abnormal vaginal discharge. The treatment group received modified Longdan Xiegan Decoction, while the control group received conventional antibiotics. After 4 weeks, the herbal group showed a significantly higher rate of improvement in discharge volume, color, and odor, as well as cervical erosion healing (P<0.05).
research.periodical: Liu Y, Zhang H, Wang J. Clinical observation on modified Longdan Xiegan Decoction in treating chronic cervicitis with damp-heat syndrome. Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine. 2015;35(8):987-990.

research.title: Guizhi Fuling Wan for pelvic inflammatory disease sequelae: A systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis included 12 RCTs with a total of 1,056 patients. Guizhi Fuling Wan combined with antibiotics significantly improved lower abdominal pain and reduced abnormal vaginal discharge compared to antibiotics alone. The formula was particularly effective for patients with blood stasis and damp-heat patterns, with a low incidence of adverse events.
research.periodical: Chen X, Li M, Zhang R. Guizhi Fuling Wan for pelvic inflammatory disease sequelae: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2018;2018:5896804.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic pelvic inflammatory disease: A systematic review
research.description: A review of 15 RCTs evaluating acupuncture as an adjunct or alternative to antibiotics for chronic PID. Acupuncture significantly improved pelvic pain and reduced leukorrhea (vaginal discharge) compared to control. The review noted that acupuncture was safe and well-tolerated, but the overall quality of evidence was low due to small sample sizes and risk of bias.
research.periodical: Li J, Wang Q, Zhao H. Acupuncture for chronic pelvic inflammatory disease: A systematic review. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2017;37(5):678-685.
